title: Spinal Cord

source.quote: the need for physical and mental stimulation. Berne called this stimulus-hunger.

setting: A short-staffed foundling home. Nurse Elena has fourteen infants to feed, clean, and move through on schedule this week. Baby Teo, six months old, is fed well and kept warm - and by the chart, he should be fine.

L1.line: He's fed, he's clean, he's warm. By every chart he should be fine.
cues: low weight gain despite full feeds
doesn't track faces or reach for the crib bars
no crying, no fussing - unusually quiet
L1.question: Teo is physically cared for but failing to thrive. Spitz saw this across a whole ward of infants like him. What's actually missing?

options.feedback: He's already being fed well and the chart confirms it - this isn't a nutrition gap, so more milk won't touch the real problem.

options.text: He needs medicine for an infection.
options.feedback: No infection was found. Spitz's infants were physically healthy by every medical measure available at the time, and many still declined.

options.text: He needs to be picked up, talked to, played with - not just fed and changed.
options.feedback: Right. Spitz called this stimulus-hunger: the need for physical and mental stimulation, separate from food, warmth, or cleanliness.

L1.lesson: Spitz's infants were fed, clean, and warm, and some still declined. Stimulus-hunger is a need in its own right, not a symptom of poor feeding - recognition has to be supplied directly, and nothing else substitutes for it.

L2.intro: It's a six-day stretch on the ward. The home is short two nurses this week. Levine's rat pups told the same story from the other direction: the ones given mild electric shocks developed better than the ones left in a featureless box with no stimulation at all. Any input beats none. What does Elena do with the little time she has?

beats.line: Feed, change, move to the next crib. We don't have hands for holding - there are thirteen more behind him.
cues: already walking to the next crib

options.text: Nod, and keep to the schedule exactly as she says.
options.outcome: Teo is fed on time all week. By Wednesday he's stopped reaching toward the crib bars when someone passes.
options.lesson: Compliance keeps the ward running, but it doesn't feed stimulus-hunger - being fed and clean was never the missing ingredient.

options.text: Steal two minutes with Teo at the end of each round - talk to him, let him grip your finger.
options.outcome: He brightens for the two minutes he has her. The other twenty-two hours are still silent.
options.lesson: Two minutes a round is real stimulation and it genuinely helps him in the moment - but one nurse's two minutes can't cover a need that has to be met continuously. A deficit this size is structural, not something one kind act fixes.

options.text: Tell Agnes the ward needs a holding rota, not more hands on bottles.
options.outcome: Agnes says she'll "raise it at the next meeting." Nothing changes by Friday.
options.lesson: The diagnosis is correct, but raising it without any power to act on it just relocates the problem upward - it feels like doing something while changing nothing for Teo this week.

beats.line: His weight's flat. Chart says healthy. I don't have a box to tick for "nobody talks to him."
cues: reading the chart, not looking at the crib

options.text: Ask him to write "needs handling, not just feeding" on the chart.
options.outcome: He writes it. It still doesn't add a nurse to the floor, but it's now on record that feeding isn't the fix.
options.lesson: Naming stimulus-hunger as a real, separate need - not a feeding problem - is the correct diagnosis, even though naming it doesn't by itself supply it.

options.text: Say nothing; it's not her place to tell a doctor his job.
options.outcome: Dr. Hale moves to the next crib. Teo is logged as "healthy, underweight, cause unclear."
options.lesson: Staying quiet keeps the peace, but it leaves the real cause - recognition deprivation - undiagnosed and untreated.

options.text: Suggest he prescribe a vitamin supplement, since that's easier to order.
options.outcome: The vitamins arrive Thursday. Teo's weight doesn't move.
options.lesson: Treating a stimulus-hunger problem as a nutrition problem is a comfortable, orderable fix that doesn't touch the actual deficit - the chart looks like something was done.

beats.line: End of the week. How's the quiet one in cot four?
cues: glancing at the clipboard, not at the crib

options.text: Tell her the truth: he's stopped crying, stopped reaching, and that's worse, not better.
options.outcome: Agnes pauses. "Spitz again," she says quietly. "Saw this in '44." For the first time all week she looks at the crib instead of the clipboard.
options.lesson: A quiet baby isn't a calm baby - Spitz's observation was that withdrawal and apathy, not crying, are the late sign of stimulus-hunger. Naming it accurately is the first thing that lets anyone act on it.

options.outcome: Agnes writes "settled" in the log. The real pattern - withdrawal - goes unrecorded for next week's nurse.
options.lesson: "Settled" and "shut down" can look identical on a clipboard; calling withdrawal "settling in" erases the exact signal that would get Teo help.

options.text: Say nothing and hope next week's staffing is better.
options.outcome: Next week's rota is the same as this one's. Hope wasn't a plan.
options.lesson: Waiting for a structural problem to fix itself doesn't meet a hunger that's active right now.

echo.setting: 72 hours later: a slow Sunday. No texts, no plans, nobody's checked in all day.
echo.shape: notice the pull to manufacture some contact, even a small one, rather than go without
